title: The user feedback loop
subtitle: Thumbs-down, human review and new cases in the set, without teaching the assistant to please
mission: The assistant is live: about 2,000 conversations a week, and around 3% get a thumbs-up or thumbs-down, sometimes with a comment. The team has 4 weeks and must decide three things: what to optimize (approval, or accuracy measured on 2026-11), how many random conversations HR reviews each week and whether failures become new evaluation cases. Build the loop and make accuracy go up.

predict.question: if the team changes the prompt every week to maximize thumbs-up, the accuracy measured on set 2026-11…

feedback.right: right: approval goes from 70% to 82% and accuracy drops from 79% to 72%. The pleasing prompt answers more confidently and refuses less, even when it should refuse.
feedback.wrong: it goes down: approval goes from 70% to 82% and accuracy drops from 79% to 72%. The pleasing prompt answers more confidently and refuses less, even when it should refuse.

why.simples:
Customer opinions are gold, but they mislead: few people complain, and many thank you for a wrong answer that sounded nice. If you change the restaurant only to get more "likes", it may start serving everyone dessert and forget the main course.
The good loop uses thumbs to find problems, has a person check a random sample, and turns every error found into a new exam question. The score that rules is still the exam’s.
why.dev:
Three sources, each with its bias: thumbs-down with a comment (low volume, lots of signal, complainer bias), human review of a random sample (finds silent failures, the ones nobody complained about) and automatic metrics on traffic (refusals, handoffs, repeated questions). Every week: a review queue with the thumbs-down + N random conversations, HR marks verdict and category, and failures become cases in a new set version (2026-12), with their origin recorded.
The product decision stays with the set: thumbs are a guardrail metric and a source of cases, not a target. Automatic triage of comments (the lesson’s one, in JSON with closed categories) helps prioritize, but "does it become a test" goes through a person. Also record what’s missing from the handbook: "daycare allowance" isn’t a prompt bug, it’s a document HR needs to write.
why.especialista:
Optimizing straight for thumbs has a public precedent. In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update that made the model sycophantic; by the company’s account, the update added a reward signal based on ChatGPT thumbs-up and thumbs-down, and the changes together weakened the main signal that had kept sycophancy in check. Offline evaluations and A/B tests didn’t catch it. The lesson for a small team is the same: approval is an easy target to inflate.
Feedback is also personal data: a comment may carry health, salary or a conflict with a manager. Decide who reads the review queue, how long logs are kept and what is anonymized before becoming a test case (replace names and numbers before saving to the set). And close the loop with whoever complained when you can: people who see their problem fixed keep giving feedback.

data.triageSys: You triage employee comments about Aurora’s HR assistant. Put the comment in one category: wrong_answer (the assistant said something wrong), missing_doc (the topic isn’t in the handbook), tone (right answer, but the way it said it bothered them), praise or other. add_to_eval is true when the case should become a test in the evaluation set (a wrong answer or a topic missing from the handbook). Reply only with JSON: {"category":"...","add_to_eval":true}.

steps:
Store every assistant conversation in a weekly JSON Lines log, with the rating and comment when there is one (replace names and personal numbers before saving). Example line of logs/2026-W46.jsonl:
{"id": "c-1042", "question": "How much of my vacation can I sell?", "answer": "Up to half your vacation.", "rating": "down", "comment": "HR said it’s one third."}

Create review_queue.py, which builds the week’s queue: every thumbs-down plus 40 random conversations (the draw uses the week as its seed, so it can be repeated):
import csv
import json
import random
import sys

week = sys.argv[1]  # e.g. 2026-W46
convs = [json.loads(line) for line in open(f"logs/{week}.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") if line.strip()]
down = [c for c in convs if c.get("rating") == "down"]
down_ids = {c["id"] for c in down}
others = [c for c in convs if c["id"] not in down_ids]
random.seed(week)
sample = random.sample(others, min(40, len(others)))

with open(f"review-{week}.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["id", "source", "question", "answer", "comment", "verdict", "category", "add_to_eval"])
    for c in down:
        w.writerow([c["id"], "thumbs_down", c["question"], c["answer"], c.get("comment", ""), "", "", ""])
    for c in sample:
        w.writerow([c["id"], "random", c["question"], c["answer"], "", "", "", ""])
print(f"{len(down)} thumbs-down + {len(sample)} random conversations in review-{week}.csv")

Run it and hand the CSV to HR, who fills in verdict (ok or wrong), category and add_to_eval (yes or no):
python review_queue.py 2026-W46

Create add_cases.py, which builds the new set version with the marked cases (the old version stays as it is):
import csv
import json
import sys

review, old, new = sys.argv[1:4]
text = open(old, encoding="utf-8").read().rstrip("\n") + "\n"
added = 0
with open(new, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    out.write(text)
    for row in csv.DictReader(open(review, encoding="utf-8")):
        if row["add_to_eval"].strip().lower() != "yes":
            continue
        case = {"id": "fb-" + row["id"], "question": row["question"], "category": row["category"], "source": row["source"]}
        out.write(json.dumps(case, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
        added += 1
print(f"{new}: {added} new cases on top of {old}")
Run:
python add_cases.py review-2026-W46.csv evals/rh/2026-11.jsonl evals/rh/2026-12.jsonl
recipe.ok: review-2026-W46.csv holds the thumbs-down plus 40 random conversations; after the review, add_cases.py creates 2026-12.jsonl with all of 2026-11 plus the cases marked yes, and the next prompt comparison uses that version on both sides.
